summary:
Papua New Guinea is dangerous for trans visitors. Sex between men is criminalised, with penalties of up to 14 years' imprisonment, and the regime of stigma and violence around it applies visibly to transgender people. The Asian Development Bank's 2024 assessment of the legal status of sexual and gender minorities across 17 countries in Asia and the Pacific includes Papua New Guinea, with decriminalisation among the topics examined, confirming that the criminal-law position remains a live legal question rather than a settled matter.

Reporting on trans and gender-diverse people in Port Moresby documents direct targeting. ABC News reported in October 2014 that gay and transgender people in the capital are commonly raped or beaten, in some cases by police officers. A 24-year-old gay man recounted being pelted with stones and bottles. Transgender people who present as women face the same exposure to this violence.

One documented pocket of safety exists: Hanuabada, a village built over the sea on Port Moresby's outskirts, where residents live openly and transgender people wear women's clothing in the street without retaliation. This is an exception, not the national pattern.

The wider accountability climate compounds the risk. Human Rights Watch has recorded police abuse, including of children, continuing with little accountability even for fatalities or egregious physical abuse, and has found that sorcery-related killings in the highlands provinces go largely unpunished, with police routinely taking no action. A visitor who is assaulted has little practical recourse.
tangentialFactors:
The violence documented against gay and transgender people in Port Moresby sits within a broader pattern of mob violence and police impunity that Human Rights Watch has recorded for years, including a 2009 case in which a mob stripped, beat and burned a woman accused of sorcery within yards of a police station.

Campaigners quoted in reporting say that attitudes toward LGBT people shift with direct exposure to the community, which is why a single village can function as a safe haven while the capital remains hostile.

Papua New Guinea's position is assessed alongside 16 other Asia-Pacific jurisdictions by the Asian Development Bank, placing its legal regime within a regional comparative framework rather than treating it as an isolated case.
localsOnly:
Residents of Hanuabada village on Port Moresby's outskirts live openly as gay and transgender people, with transgender residents wearing women's clothing in public without retaliation, according to ABC News and Guardian reporting.

Outside such enclaves, gay and transgender residents of Port Moresby face routine rape and beatings, sometimes at the hands of police officers.

Provincial commanders recorded more than 50 sorcery-related killings in two highlands provinces in 2008, with perpetrators rarely brought to justice; sorcery accusations, sometimes linked to HIV deaths, have been used to conceal murders and mitigate sentences.
outOfScopeNotes:
The precise statutory provision and current penalty for sex between men in Papua New Guinea are not stated in the sourced inventory beyond the figure of up to 14 years' imprisonment; the exact offence and any recent amendment are unresolved.

No sourced material in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, marker changes on documents, passport or visa rules for trans travellers, access to gender-affirming healthcare, or hate-crime provisions specific to gender identity in Papua New Guinea. These remain not sourced.

The inventory does not establish whether the Asian Development Bank's 2024 assessment recommends or records any change to Papua New Guinea's decriminalisation status; only that the topic was examined.
